name: Affective forecasting
statement: People overestimate how strongly and how long a future event will move them, an error that shrinks or disappears when they are asked about their feelings towards the event itself.
meaning: Three separate claims travel under this heading and they are not interchangeable. The durability bias says predicted feelings last longer than real ones. The impact bias is the wider claim, covering initial intensity as well as duration. Wilson and Gilbert say in their 2013 comment that they coined the durability bias in 1998, then widened the term to impact bias in a 2002 chapter once it became clear that people mispredict their initial reactions too. Immune neglect is the third claim, and it is an explanation rather than a finding. It holds that people run a set of unnoticed defences, rationalisation, reappraisal, blame-shifting, which Gilbert and colleagues call the psychological immune system, and that forecasters do not allow for it. Only the first two are measured directly. The immune system is inferred from a pattern: forecasters predict the same reaction to two versions of an event, and experiencers react less to the version their defences can attack. A fourth idea, that intense distress can lift faster than mild distress because only intense distress trips those defences, is the region-beta paradox and has its own entry.

origin.who: Daniel T. Gilbert, Elizabeth C. Pinel, Timothy D. Wilson, Stephen J. Blumberg and Thalia P. Wheatley
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Six studies covering a romantic breakup, a tenure decision, a lost election, negative personality feedback, a story about an infant's death, and a job rejection. The paper names the durability bias and immune neglect; the phrase impact bias appears nowhere in it.

evidence: Study 1 surveyed 571 undergraduates at the University of Texas at Austin and analysed 532. Students who had never been through a breakup predicted their happiness two months after one at 3.89 on a seven-point scale. Students who had actually been through one sat at 5.46 if it was old and 5.42 if it was recent, against 5.27 for those who had not, F(1, 529) = 125.76 and 40.70 for the two comparisons with the forecast, both p < .001. The matching positive forecast was accurate: students expecting to be lovers guessed 5.79 and lovers reported 5.71 and 5.91, both contrasts null. Study 2 posted questionnaires to faculty and got 33 forecasters, 47 who had won tenure and 20 who had not. Forecasters put their happiness at 3.42 in the five years after being denied tenure. The seven recent denials reported 4.71, F(1, 38) = 4.36, p = .04, and the 13 older denials matched the forecast, F(1, 44) = 0.20. Study 3 stopped 57 voters leaving a polling station in the 1994 Texas gubernatorial election and reached 25 of them a month later, 10 losers and 15 winners. Losers predicted 4.90 and reported 4.40, F(1, 23) = 7.84, p < .02; winners were accurate. Across the first three studies the paper reports a mean effect size for the negative durability bias between r = .38 and .41, and between r = .02 and .12 for the positive one. Studies 4 to 6 staged failure in a laboratory. Study 4 gave 70 analysable students a mundane personality classification from a fallible or an infallible source. Among the 32 with positive self-views, forecasts ignored the source and experiences did not, interaction F(1, 30) = 5.26, p < .03, though the three-way interaction that defines the design was F(1, 62) = 3.37, p = .071. Study 5 gave 143 women at the University of Virginia a fabricated newspaper story about an infant suffocating in a playpen, blamelessly or through negligence. Forecasters, 114 of them, expected equal upset; the 29 experiencers were less upset by the blameworthy version, F(1, 139) = 3.84, p = .05. Study 6 rejected 78 analysable women for a mock job by a fair or an unfair procedure. The 39 who both forecast and experienced predicted the same misery either way and, ten minutes later, the unfairly rejected felt better, F(1, 37) = 6.14, p = .018.

replication.headline: The overestimation is large and reliable when people are later asked how they feel in general, and about zero when they are asked how they feel about the event.
replication.detail: Levine, Lench, Kaplan and Safer meta-analysed 84 affective forecasting studies from 44 sources, 156 effect sizes and 9,870 participants, searching PsycINFO to the end of 2010. The pooled overestimate was Hedges's g = 0.55, 95% CI [0.42, 0.68], with heterogeneity Q = 606.73, p < .001. Splitting studies by how the experience question was worded and timed moved the number a long way, QB(3) = 40.70, p < .001. A general question after a delay, the standard procedure, gave g = 0.80, 95% CI [0.65, 0.95]. A general question asked immediately gave 0.16, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.36]. A question naming the event gave 0.37, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.78] after a delay and -0.01, 95% CI [-0.28, 0.26] immediately. None of those three differed from zero. Their four experiments make the same point on one event at a time. Of 394 students forecasting the 2008 presidential election, those later asked how happy they felt in general showed the usual gap, g = 0.48 for Obama supporters and 1.44 for McCain supporters, while those asked how happy they felt about the result showed g = 0.17 and 0.05. Asked afterwards how they had read the general question, 75% and 81% of 99 students picked an event-specific paraphrase over a mood paraphrase. Wilson and Gilbert replied that the meta-analysis omitted whole literatures, miscoded studies and pooled conditions designed to cancel. Recoding the seven specific-immediate studies, the category that best tests the claim, they get g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.16, 0.84], p = .004, against Levine's -0.01. Dropping the four contested studies instead leaves five with g = 0.35, 95% CI [0.20, 0.51], p < .001. Levine and colleagues answered with recomputed contrasts. Using Wilson and Gilbert's own coding of the specific-immediate studies, the general-delayed effect stays the larger of the two, QB(1) = 4.51, p = .03, and the specific-immediate effect does not differ from the 27 other studies that used specific or immediate questions, QB(1) = 0.40, p = .53. Dropping the studies whose designs were meant to lessen the bias moves the four-way contrast from QB(3) = 40.70 to QB(3) = 27.18, still p < .001. They titled the reply to say the impact bias is both dead and alive. Panel studies test the durability half against real outcomes rather than against a forecast made in a laboratory. Luhmann, Hofmann, Eid and Lucas pooled 188 publications, 313 samples and 65,911 people across eight life events. For unemployment the prospective intercept was b0 = -0.43, 95% CI [-0.48, -0.38], and cognitive well-being then rose at b1 = 0.12, 95% CI [0.10, 0.13]. For divorce the intercept was b0 = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.13, -0.01] and the slope b1 = 0.07, 95% CI [0.05, 0.08]. Lucas followed 679 people through the onset of a long-term disability inside a panel of 39,987, for an average of 7.18 years before and 7.39 years after onset, and 272 people inside a second panel of 27,406. He reports drops in happiness of 0.40 to 1.27 standard deviations, followed by little adaptation over time.

study.cite: Levine, L. J., Lench, H. C., Kaplan, R. L., & Safer, M. A. (2012). Accuracy and artifact: Reexamining the intensity bias in affective forecasting. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 103(4), 584-605.

limits: No direct repetition of the six 1998 studies was located. Searches covered Crossref, Europe PMC for 'durability bias', 'immune neglect' and 'impact bias' paired with replication and preregistration terms, PubMed and general web searches; OpenAlex was rate-limited before a citation sweep could be run and PsycINFO was not searched. A later pass queried the OSF registry, which returned 28 registrations for 'affective forecasting' and two for 'impact bias', and none of those titles describes a repetition of the 1998 protocol. Two of the three claims rest on thin designs. Studies 1 and 2 are cross-sectional, so the forecasters and the experiencers are different people, and the paper says so. Study 2's key comparison uses seven people. Study 3 reached 25 of 57 voters. The immune neglect studies turn on interactions that did not reach significance: F(1, 62) = 3.37, p = .071 in Study 4, a null role by story interaction of F(1, 139) = 1.33, p = .25 in Study 5, and p = .181 in Study 6, with the supporting contrasts run regardless. Study 5 compared 114 forecasters against 29 experiencers. Nothing in Studies 4 to 6 tracked affect for more than ten minutes, so the durability claim is carried by the three cross-sectional studies. Patel and Urry gave 173 people a navigation task after assigning them to reappraise, suppress or do nothing, reasoning that a working immune system should shrink forecasting error. Error was the same in all three conditions. Hoerger's Valentine's Day study of 325 young adults runs the other way: effective coping correlated with experienced emotion up to r = .63 but with predicted emotion no higher than .15, and the gap was larger on the day itself than after it, Z = 2.68, p = .01. Mathieu and Gosling's argument that forecasts look accurate or inaccurate depending on the index used could not be obtained; the only figure quoted here from it, an average forecast-experience correlation of r = .28, is taken from Wilson and Gilbert's description. Medical evidence points both ways. Van den Bosch and colleagues screened 5,726 records and found seven empirical comparisons of predicted against actual emotion in patients, concluding that people exaggerate both anticipated joy and anticipated grief. Panda and colleagues followed 74 cancer surgery patients from 2017 to 2019 and found the opposite direction, patients expecting better quality of life than they got, with correlations between expected and experienced trends at or below 0.4 in six of eight domains. Everyday events produce smaller errors than the famous ones. Moeck, Grewal, Mehta, Greenaway, Koval and Kalokerinos ran a week-long experience sampling study with 209 people, on scales whose error index runs from 100 for maximum overestimation to -100 for maximum underestimation. Forecasts of the next day's positive affect ran above that evening's retrospective rating by 2.07, 95% CI [1.13, 3.01]. Forecast negative affect ran above the day's average of nine momentary ratings by 5.73, 95% CI [4.95, 6.52], and matched the evening's retrospective rating, -0.19, 95% CI [-1.09, 0.71], p = .684. In their two-week diary, 69 people nominated an unpleasant event each day and overestimated the negative affect it brought, 0.16, 95% CI [0.11, 0.22], while forecasting less pleasure than they felt, -0.15, 95% CI [-0.23, -0.06]. Buechel, Zhang and Morewedge argue the direction of the error is not fixed at all. Their abstract reports forecasters underestimating the impact of a smaller prize they expected to win and of a short unpleasant video about a distant event, and overestimating a larger prize they did not expect and a long video about a near event. Adaptation itself is partial, which matters because the popular version of the claim assumes it is complete. Lucas, Clark, Georgellis and Diener followed more than 24,000 Germans for 15 years and report people reacting strongly to unemployment and then shifting back without regaining their former satisfaction, even once reemployed. Lucas's 18-year panel of more than 30,000 Germans shows satisfaction falling as divorce approaches and rebounding afterwards, again without completing the return.
misreadings: The lottery study behind the popular retelling does not say what the retelling says. Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman interviewed 22 Illinois lottery winners, 22 controls drawn from the phone book and 29 accident victims, 11 paraplegic and 18 quadriplegic, all recruited at one rehabilitation institute. Response rates were 52%, 41% and 85%. On six-point scales the victims rated their present happiness at 2.96 against 3.82 for controls, F(1, 47) = 7.16, p < .01. They were significantly less happy, not equally happy, and the accurate half of the story is that winners at 4.00 did not differ from controls, F = 0.27. Ten of the 29 victims declined the question about future happiness. No repetition of that study was located, and the closest modern equivalent points the other way. Lindqvist, Ostling and Cesarini surveyed Swedish lottery players 5 to 22 years after a major lottery event, following preregistered procedures. Their abstract reports that large-prize winners gained overall life satisfaction against matched controls, that the gain persisted for over a decade with no sign of dissipating, and that the estimated effects on happiness and mental health were significantly smaller. Overestimating intensity and overestimating duration are separate errors with separate evidence, and every effect size in the Levine meta-analysis is an intensity rating rather than a duration estimate. Immune neglect is a third thing again, an account of why the error happens, and no study in the 1998 paper measured a defence directly. The 1998 authors anticipated the wording objection and dismissed it, arguing that a forecaster who forgets an event will fade from mind is showing focalism rather than answering a badly built question. Levine and colleagues turned that into a testable difference and found that most people read 'in general, how happy will you feel' as a question about the event. On the shared reading, forecasts of feelings about an event are close to accurate and forecasts of general mood are not.
